idiom_name: Slick lifted table class (Table[...] with column[T]("..."))
implementation_notes: Metadata is a class per table extending Table[...] with a Tag parameter: def name = column[String]("COF_NAME", O.PrimaryKey) fixes the Scala type, the SQL column name and column options, the default projection * declares the row shape, and TableQuery[T] is the queryable table. Slick is reader and engine - the lifted embedding compiles those column definitions into SQL and expects or returns the projection type, and the same definitions generate DDL - so the column knowledge exists once and no hand-written mapper is needed; mapped tables with mapTo or the <> operator bind the projection to a case class. Choose it when the table should be an explicit object; choose doobie when the mapping should come from the types and the query should stay as SQL in a pure FP stack.
pitfalls: The * projection is the mapping: a column added to the table but not to the projection returns rows in the wrong shape rather than failing to compile in every case.
Mapping functions must be total and lossless: a partially applied case class or a lossy <> pair fails at run time.
Profile and implicit imports select dialect and column types, so mixing profiles in one project produces confusing type errors and inconsistent DDL.

variants.name: doobie Read/Write derived from case classes
variants.idiom_name: doobie Read[A]/Write[A] derivation over case classes
variants.implementation_notes: Here the store is the type itself: for a case class doobie derives Read[A] and Write[A] (implicit derivation, with Read.derived available on Scala 3 and opt-in automatic derivation enabled by an import), mapping fields onto JDBC columns positionally, and custom instances in scope override the default where a column is named or typed differently. doobie is a pure functional JDBC layer rather than an ORM, so the type classes are the mapping and the connectionIO fragments are the query: domain types stay free of persistence declarations and the mapping is a value the compiler resolves. Use it in Cats-effect stacks; Slick fits better when the table should be an explicit object.
pitfalls: Derivation is positional: reordering case-class fields silently reinterprets columns whose JDBC types coincide.
Implicit instances are easy to lose: a missing or duplicated Read/Write in scope changes the mapping or fails to compile with an error that points at the query.
